newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Arrests put fresh pressure on Belgian governmment.
newsitem.headline: Arrests put fresh pressure on Belgian governmment.

text.p: The Belgian government, already enmeshed in a series of political scandals, has been put under renewed pressure by the arrest of two Socialist Party (PS) officials.

Merry Hermanus and Francois Pirot, two former top officials of the francophone party, were arrested last week as part of a probe into allegations that the PS received kickbacks from French aviation firm Dassault.
The PS is part of a four-party centre-left coalition government with the Flemish Socialists and the French and Flemish Christian Democratic parties.
Several opposition members called on Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, a Christian Democrat, to drop the French socialists and call an election.

At the weekly meeting of his Flemish CVP party on Monday, Dehaene ducked reporters' questions about the government's stability. Later he told Belgian radio BRTN that it was up to the courts to clarify the case.

"Corruption has never been admissible in this country, there can be no pardon for that," he said. "I hope some parties will clean up their affairs," he added, clearly sniping at the PS which has alreay been linked to other political scandals.

Belgian media said Hermanus and Pirot had admitted receiving 30 million Belgian francs (about $1 million) from Dassault in 1989, in exchange for help in securing a contract to fit the Belgian army's F-16 fighter jets with air defence systems.

"In a letter to me Mr. Hermanus said that the PS has received 30 million francs," PS vice-chairman Philippe Moureaux told RTL television on Monday, adding that he had no means of verifying this and he had passed the letter to the judiciary.
But PS chairman Philippe Busquin denied that the party had received kickbacks. "I became chairman in 1992. I have no knowledge of this," he told RTL.
Asked whether his party had enough credibility to remain in the government, Busquin said: "Please do not confuse the current Parti Socialiste with the PS of the late eighties."
Charles-Ferdinand Nothomb, the leader of the francophone Christian Democratic Party PSC told RTL he was waiting to see what the PS did to put its house in order.
"Our party has never received anything from...Dassault," he said.
The PS -- the biggest party in the francophone southern half of Belgium and the second-biggest partner in the four-party government -- has been dogged by scandals in the past years.

In January 1994, three PS government ministers had to resign over accusations of their involvement in bribes allegedly paid by Italian helicopter maker Agusta in the late eighties. Agusta has denied all wrong doing.
One of them, former Walloon regional government president Guy Spitaels, has fought back to become chairman of the Walloon regional parliament.
Opposition parties have called for Spitaels, who was PS party chairman in the late eighties, to resign.
Asked about this his successor Busquin said: "That is his responsibility."
